items.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.  CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers […]
items.content:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.  

 CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.  

 At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. 

 From SC06 to SC26 

 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. 

 In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films .  

 Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack.  

 Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 

 Honoring the Architects of Progress 

 Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: 

 At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. 

 In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.  

 That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution . 

 These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more. 

 Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26 .

items.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
items.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.  As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next […]
items.content:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.  

 As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. 

 The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. 

 Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 

 Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. 

 “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”  

 Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery 

 Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.  

 To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.  

 That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.  

 These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

 Accelerate Molecular Dynamics Simulations with Accurate, Flexible Primitives Using NVIDIA cuPotential

 By Yutong Zhao , Darren Hsu and Kris Kersten

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA cuPotential provides modular C API primitives that accelerate molecular dynamics simulations by optimizing long-range interaction evaluation under periodic boundary conditions.
 The library integrates with OpenMM through a plugin that replaces the nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat with drop-in replacements requiring minimal code changes.
 Benchmarks across GPU architectures from T4 to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell show end-to-end speedups of 2x to over 3x for systems ranging from 24,000 to 400,000 atoms under NPT conditions.
 New C2 continuous splitting and spreading functions developed with D. E. Shaw Research and the Flatiron Institute achieve target accuracy at lower grid resolutions and reduced cutoffs compared to standard Ewald and u-series methods.
 Energy drift measurements over 10 ns show cuPotential reduces drift by several hundred fold versus default PME settings, exceeding typical biomolecular simulation requirements.
 Beyond electrostatics, the library improves dispersion energy accuracy by several thousand fold while maintaining comparable force errors at lower computational cost.
 Next Steps
 Visit the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repository to access examples, benchmarks, and integration code.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 Molecular dynamics (MD) is an indispensable tool across physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Owing to its arithmetic structure, particularly the parallel evaluation of many atom-pair interactions, MD codes were among the first to be ported to run on GPUs. However, as GPUs evolve, optimizing kernels and ensuring compatibility across heterogeneous hardware have become more difficult than ever for many MD engine developers.

 Specifically, in simulations run with classical forcefields, the evaluation of long-range interactions under periodic boundary conditions, such as electrostatics and dispersion, remains the major computational and engineering bottleneck.

 NVIDIA cuPotential , a focused library designed for molecular dynamics, addresses these challenges. By offering modular primitives with a C API, cuPotential empowers developers and users to select specific components from multiple layers of the stack to accelerate workloads (Figure 1).

 cuPotential provides direct space and reciprocal space utilities such as cutoff-based interaction evaluators and charge spreading functions. This release also provides a plugin specifically for OpenMM given its popularity in the developer ecosystem as an example. The goal is seamless drop-in replacements with minimal changes to the user’s code.

 This post explains how to integrate the plugin into OpenMM, evaluate accuracy against high-accuracy references, and measure simulation throughput. It also introduces two examples for developers who need control over parameter representation and updates. Finally, it briefly discusses the science and error analysis behind the new splitting and spreading methods. This rigorous attention to accuracy and energy drift in simulation allows developers to integrate and benefit from the acceleration provided by cuPotential kernels without affecting simulation results.

 Figure 1. cuPotential library stacks can be integrated into MD engines such as OpenMM through a C API 

 Building the cuPotential runtime and plugin for OpenMM 

 cuPotential is composed of two parts: a core methods library and a plugin for OpenMM that consumes the primitives that can be built directly in a conda environment on Linux. The following tutorial walks through building the runtime and plugin, installing the Python wheel, and running the supplied molecular dynamics sample.

 Prerequisites 

 Linux x86-64 with a supported NVIDIA GPU

 An installed NVIDIA driver compatible with CUDA 13.1

 Conda or Micromamba installed and initialized for your shell

 A clone of the cuPotential repository from the NVIDIA/cuPotential GitHub repo

 The environment supplies the CUDA toolkit and compilers; a separate system-wide CUDA toolkit installation is not required. The GPU driver must already be installed on the host.

 Step 1: Create and activate the environment 

 Using Conda, create and activate the environment:

conda create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \
 python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \
 cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \
 cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \
 swig pip setuptools wheel numpy

conda activate cupotential-build

 Alternatively, you can use Micromamba:

micromamba create -y -n cupotential-build -c conda-forge \
 python=3.12 openmm=8.4.0 \
 cuda-version=13.1 cuda-toolkit=13.1 \
 cmake make gcc_linux-64=13 gxx_linux-64=13 \
 swig pip setuptools wheel numpy

micromamba activate cupotential-build

 Next, install the Python build dependencies:

python -m pip install "pybind11>=2.12" nvidia-mathdx

 The cuda-toolkit package supplies the CUDA compiler and development tools. Setting cuda-version alone does not install those tools.

 Step 2: Point the build helper to the active environment 

 In plugins/openmm/run_build , replace:

OPENMM=/opt/openmm

 with:

OPENMM="${CONDA_PREFIX:?Activate the conda environment first}"

 Both Conda and Micromamba set CONDA_PREFIX when an environment is activated.

 Step 3: Build and install 

 Use the cuPotential repository root, with the environment active:

export CUDACXX="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/nvcc"
export CUDAHOSTCXX="$CXX"

./plugins/openmm/run_build
python -m pip wheel \
 --no-deps --no-build-isolation \
 --wheel-dir plugins/openmm/dist \
 ./plugins/openmm
python -m pip install plugins/openmm/dist/*.whl

 The build helper compiles the cuPotential runtime if it’s not already present, then builds the OpenMM plugin. The final installation command also installs the wheel’s declared pip CUDA dependencies.

 Step 4: Verify the installation 

 Run the supplied sample directly:

cd plugins/openmm/samples
./solvated_systems/run

 The sample evaluates DHFR (Dihydrofolate reductase), BACE (Beta-secretase 1), and ApoA1 (Apolipoprotein A1), under both NVT and NPT conditions. The DHFR and ApoA1 systems are from the OpenMM benchmark suite , while BACE is from the OpenFE benchmark set . A successful run ends with:

PASS

 The samples use AMBER14/TIP3P force field, a 0.9 nm nonbonded interaction cutoff length, a 5 x 10⁻⁴ electrostatic accuracy target, and mixed precision. Its 4 fs timestep is paired with constrained hydrogen bonds, rigid water, and hydrogen mass repartitioning to 1.5 amu.

 These runs measure accuracy and performance separately. For electrostatics, it compares both implementations with a double-precision reference, using twice the cutoff length for the short range part and twice the mesh resolution in each dimension for the long range part, with the Ewald splitting parameter held fixed. For truncated Lennard-Jones interactions, it uses a double-precision reference at the same cutoff, preserving the interaction model being tested.

 For throughput, each implementation runs 500 warm-up steps followed by 3,000 timed steps. The cuPotential arm uses its own force and integrator, plus its barostat for NPT. The reported speedup therefore describes that integrated configuration.

 Using cuPotential with OpenMM 

 The cuPotential OpenMM plugin provides replacements for the OpenMM nonbonded force, Langevin integrator, and Monte Carlo barostat. In your production MD simulations, the key steps to integrate cuPotential into OpenMM are:

 Replace the system’s OpenMM nonbonded force before creating the simulation context

 Use integrator and optionally barostat from cuPotential

import openmm as mm
import openmm.unit as unit
import nv_openmm_plugin as nv

temperature = 300 * unit.kelvin # Temperature, 300 K
timestep = 0.004 * unit.picoseconds # Timestep, 4 fs
friction_coeff = 1.0 / unit.picoseconds # Friction coefficient in Langevin thermostat
pressure = 1.0 * unit.bar # Pressure if using barostat for NPT

# Prepare the system using OpenMM. Replace with your system.
pdb = app.PDBFile("solvated.pdb")
forcefield = app.ForceField("amber14-all.xml", "amber14/tip3p.xml")

system = forcefield.createSystem(
 pdb.topology,
 nonbondedMethod=app.PME,
 nonbondedCutoff=0.9 * unit.nanometers,
 ewaldErrorTolerance=5e-4,
 constraints=app.HBonds,
 rigidWater=True,
 hydrogenMass=1.5 * unit.amu,
)

# replace OpenMM NonbondedForce instance with the plugin's NonbondedForce
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()):
 if isinstance(force, mm.NonbondedForce):
 system.addForce(nv.NonbondedForce(force))
 system.removeForce(index)
 break

# The cuPotential integrator handles center-of-mass motion removal.
for index, force in enumerate(system.getForces()):
 if isinstance(force, mm.CMMotionRemover):
 system.removeForce(index)
 break

integrator = nv.LangevinMiddleIntegrator(
 temperature,
 friction_coeff,
 timestep,
)
# Optionally, add cuPotential barostat for NPT simulations
system.addForce(nv.MonteCarloBarostat(
 pressure, # Pressure
 temperature, # Match the integrator temperature.
 frequency=25, # Attempt a volume change every 25 steps.
))

# Create the simulation after configuring all forces.
simulation = app.Simulation(
 pdb.topology,
 system,
 integrator,
 mm.Platform.getPlatformByName("CUDA"),
 {"Precision": "mixed"},
)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy() # OpenMM 8.4 only
simulation.context.setVelocitiesToTemperature(temperature)

simulation.step(1000)

 This excerpt shows that the integration changes. The complete sample includes system construction, CUDA context creation, accuracy checks, and timing. For NPT simulations, it also uses nv.MonteCarloBarostat .

 AI-Generated Summary

 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model that delivers frontier-level accuracy on scientific benchmarks and the fastest time to solution for scientific coding.
 The Nemotron RL Litmus-Bench V2.0 dataset and benchmark trains and evaluates LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties.
 A practical recipe post-trains Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases by building a custom reinforcement learning environment from experimental data using NeMo Gym and applying RL with NVIDIA NeMo RL.
 In a drug-metabolism prediction example, supervised fine-tuning improved accuracy by 12% and RL post-training lifted it a further 17% at a 16,384-token output budget.
 An optional distillation step uses a stronger teacher model such as Claude Sonnet 5.5 to generate high-quality reasoning traces that warm-start the student model before RL, accelerating convergence.

 Use the recipe as an example to build and evaluate an environment for a specific scientific task.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 Agentic AI is reshaping scientific research and innovation. Researchers communicate complex scientific hypotheses in natural language and let autonomous agents independently plan tasks, execute simulations, evaluate results, and self-correct across multiple iterations. Scientific agents are taking on longer, more complex, and increasingly visual workflows. 

 Accuracy and inference efficiency matter at every step. Without verification, errors compound across the workflow, while latency and compute costs multiply with continued operation.

 NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a collection of models, datasets, tools, and recipes for accelerating agentic scientific workloads, addresses these hurdles. It includes Nemotron 3.5 Super VL —an open, customizable, multimodal mode l for these specialized workflows—and the NVIDIA Nemotron Litmus-Bench V2.0 , an open source chemistry-reasoning dataset and benchmark that was designed to train and evaluate LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. Out of the box, Nemotron delivers frontier level accuracy for scientific benchmarks (see Figure 1 below), along with the fastest time to solution for scientific coding.

 Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL accuracy results across several scientific benchmarks (higher is better) 

 An important benefit of Nemotron models is NVIDIA post-training support. You can customize models for your specific research domain to increase accuracy.

 This blog provides a practical recipe for post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases. Starting from a raw experimental dataset, you’ll walk through how to build a custom reinforcement learning (RL) environment using NVIDIA NeMo Gym , apply RL, and measure improvement using molecular similarity scoring. NeMo Gym supplies the environment infrastructure, and NVIDIA NeMo RL supplies the post-training framework. 

 This guide uses drug-metabolism prediction as a practical example. Given a parent compound, the starting molecule, and its transforming enzyme, the model predicts the resulting metabolite. The examples below use records from MetxBioDB, which is a comprehensive database of experimentally confirmed biotransformation reactions.

 The blog first describes direct RL, then an optional distillation step that can be used before RL when a teacher model provides useful examples.

 Build the reinforcement learning environment from experimental data 

 The starting point is a CSV file of existing experimental records such as sequences, Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, reaction conditions, and any other metadata paired with measured properties or outcomes. In this example, molecular structures are represented as SMILES strings, a text notation for describing a molecule’s atoms and bonds.

 These input-output pairs are reformatted as question-answer or user/assistant prompt pairs, with the experimental ground truth serving as a verifier to score the model’s responses. This setup constitutes a basic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) environment and requires no human preference labelling: The reward signal comes directly from the data. 

 The fidelity of that reward signal can be tuned to the task. A simple sequence-similarity function works as a lightweight verifier, while more sophisticated tools like cheminformatics libraries, molecular simulators, or even a live autonomous lab can be a tool call and can all be wired in as the environment’s scoring layer. The richer the tool, the more precisely the model is steered toward chemically or biologically meaningful outputs.

 For the metabolism example, the model receives the parent molecule and enzyme, then submits a predicted metabolite. The verifier compares the predicted and reference molecular fingerprints—numerical representations of structural features—using Tanimoto similarity. Tanimoto similarity is a metric used to measure the overlap between two sets or binary vectors and is calculated by dividing the size of their intersection by the size of their union. For the bit fingerprints used here, the score ranges from 0 to 1; higher scores indicate more similar fingerprints.

 Figure 2. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL post-training workflow 

 Direct RL post-training on the custom environment 

 With the environment in place, fine-tune the model using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with low rank adapters (LoRA). The environment presents the model with an experimental input and asks it to reason through the problem step-by-step before submitting a predicted answer via a tool call. Each submission is scored automatically by the verifier, giving a dense reward signal that requires no further annotation. The training loop, reward server, harness, and rollout workers are fully self-contained, so the same pipeline generalizes to any domain that can return a scalar reward. 

 At a 16,384-token output budget on the drug-metabolism RLVR environment, supervised fine tuning (SFT) improved the accuracy of Nemotron for Science by 12% and RL post-trained lifted it a further 17%. It demonstrates that even a highly capable instruction-tuned model continues to improve meaningfully when given targeted RL feedback on a domain-specific task.

 Figure 3. This chart shows mean molecular similarity before and after post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. 

 Distillation from stronger models as a “warm-start” for RL 

 If the base model needs a capability boost before RL training or if RL convergence is slow, a distillation step can provide significant lift. A stronger teacher model (e.g. a larger frontier model or a specialist) is run against the same environment to generate high-quality reasoning traces. A reasoning trace is high quality if the teacher model’s step-by-step logic for identifying the enzyme, predicting the reaction site, and deriving the metabolite structure leads to a SMILES that matches the ground truth metabolite. It is a low-quality reasoning trace even if the reasoning looks fluent and plausible but has some flawed logic that resulted in the wrong prediction. 

 The high-quality reasoning traces are used to fine-tune the student model via SFT or direct on-policy distillation, giving it a much better starting point before the RL loop begins. This is known as a “warm-start” and it typically accelerates convergence and raises the performance floor, making the subsequent RL training more efficient and more likely to find a strong policy.

 Data distillation for SFT 

 The distillation pipeline runs Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 across the training set, scores each rollout by Tanimoto similarity (tool call) to the ground truth metabolite, and keeps only the (question, reasoning trace) pairs where the model got it right. Those become the SFT corpus for the smaller model.

 In this environment 1,123 high-quality reasoning traces were filtered from 1,934 training prompts at Tanimoto threshold  ≥ 0.7. Here is a distilled reasoning trace for a question-answer pair from Claude Sonnet 5.5. Note that a fixed system prompt is included with every request, which can be varied across environments. LLM requests are formatted as chat messages containing both the question and the system prompt.

 MetxBioDB environment (CYP1A2 N-demethylation)

 Question:

Parent compound SMILES: Cc1nn(C)c(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C Metabolising enzyme: CYP1A2 Reason through this biotransformation step by step, then call submit_metabolite with the predicted SMILES of the primary metabolite.

 Ground truth:

Cc1[nH]nc(Cl)c1C(O)=Nc1cccc2c1C(C)OC2(C)C — Tanimoto similarity = 1.0 (exact match)

 System prompt:

You are an expert computational chemist specializing in drug metabolism. Your task is to predict the SMILES string of the metabolite produced when a given parent compound is biotransformed by a specified enzyme or enzyme family. Response format: 1. Provide step-by-step scientific reasoning: a. Identify the functional groups in the parent compound relevant to the enzyme. b. Describe the enzyme's known reaction mechanism and regioselectivity. c. Identify the specific site of biotransformation and explain why. d. Describe the chemical transformation applied (e.g. hydroxylation, glucuronidation). e. State the resulting structural change to the parent SMILES. 2. Finish by calling the submit_metabolite tool with your predicted metabolite SMILES. Rules: - The SMILES passe

 Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference 

 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores , and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions.

 Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance 

 Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline.

 For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1.

 NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run.  At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack.

 Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it 

 MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark , Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. All blog posts

 Research

 Published 11/16/2026 

 Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler

 Together Compiler uses AI agents to rewrite and fuse the GPU kernels in a model’s forward pass. It beats hand-written megakernels by 28% on B200 (2,118 vs 1,649 tokens/s on Llama 3.2 1B). This is how we got from one to the other.

 Authors

 Dylan Lim, Reyna Abhyankar, Simran Arora

 Table of contents

 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

 Introduction
 AI inference is becoming increasingly heterogeneous. New model architectures are released every week, inference traffic shifts across different batch sizes and sequence lengths, and hardware platforms continue to proliferate. Achieving peak performance across all these regimes demands optimization frameworks that can keep up.
 Last year, we helped release some of the first AI megakernels , where we executed an entire model forward pass within a single, highly fused GPU kernel. They reached record breaking speeds, but it was difficult to put them in production. After months of effort, we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer.
 This year, we examined what we could simplify and discovered something surprising. With just CUDA Graphs and PDL on top of default Torch Inductor kernels, we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel. And with “multi-kernels” and agent loops, we could further beat our old megakernels by up to 1.7x, achieving over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100.
 For the past two years, we've been investigating what a next-generation system for inference optimization should look like. After building a series of GPU programming and optimization systems, we arrived at Together Compiler, our framework for continual AI inference optimization. In this blog, we'll revisit the assumptions behind today's compilers, share the experiments that challenged our thinking, and explain the lessons that shaped Together Compiler. Our journey spans three parts:
 In Part 1, we show that Torch Compile’s heuristics and benchmarking leave performance on the table, providing motivation to build something radically different.
 In Part 2, we revisit the megakernels we built to close that gap, explain why they are not always the right optimization target, and decompose their performance gains into simpler primitives.
 In Part 3, we share our “bitter lessons” from crafting agent-driven optimization infrastructure and the final production system we ended up with.

 Together Compiler’s journey, coming to a theater near you! 
 Part 1: Torch Compile
 For over a decade, PyTorch has been the foundation of AI development, providing modular, easy-to-use abstractions ( nn.Module ) that have enabled rapid experimentation. But this modularity comes at a performance cost: executing models as sequences of individual operations can introduce substantial launch overhead, limit opportunities to overlap computation and memory movement, and leave GPU resources underutilized. To address these inefficiencies, PyTorch introduced Torch Compile (“PyTorch 2.0,” powered by Inductor) to optimize and fuse operations, while NVIDIA developed CUDA Graphs to reduce kernel launch overhead. These systems have made enormous progress, but substantial performance gaps remain, often motivating Together’s researchers to invent specialized implementations such as FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and Megakernels.
 We start with a brief overview of how Torch Compile works, then present our findings from investigating Inductor’s internals on Llama 1B.
 How Torch Compile Works
 At a high level, Torch Compile uses a just-in-time compilation pipeline to capture PyTorch operations into a computation graph, optimize that graph, and generate executable GPU kernels. The key components are:
 Graph capture. TorchDynamo traces Python execution to capture tensor operations in an intermediate representation called an FX graph. During tracing, it uses fake tensors , which carry metadata such as shapes, data types, and strides without allocating or computing the underlying tensor data. This allows the compiler to reason about the computation without actually executing it on the GPU. The resulting FX graph can be transformed and optimized before code generation.
 Operations and kernels. Inductor lowers the captured graph into its own intermediate representation, where operations are organized into categories such as pointwise (e.g., activations), reductions (e.g., summations and softmax), scans (e.g., cumulative sums), and templates (e.g., GEMMs and other specialized compute kernels). Some operations instead invoke existing implementations from libraries such as cuBLAS or custom PyTorch operators. Inductor represents these as external kernels ( ExternKernel ), whose implementations are generally opaque to its fusion machinery.
 Fusion and optimization. Inductor uses a greedy, pairwise algorithm to decide which operations to fuse into the same kernel. Its can_fuse() function checks whether a candidate fusion is legal, while score_fusion() ranks opportunities using heuristics such as estimated memory traffic savings. The algorithm repeatedly applies profitable fusions, potentially combining many operations into a single kernel. However, these decisions are based on local heuristics rather than a global search over all possible kernel partitions and execution strategies. For example, Inductor may avoid fusing operations that share no memory accesses, even when executing their work together could improve GPU utilization.
 On our target Llama 1B workload, Inductor delivers 669 TPS. As we’ll show in Part 2, these generated kernels are sometimes enough, and with small modifications, they can reach similar levels of performance to megakernels. However, on different architectures and newer hardware, Inductor’s heuristics can’t keep up. We investigated where Inductor struggles most and present three findings.
 Finding #1: Compiler heuristics cannot reliably select the best implementation across workloads.
 Inductor exposes a number of compiler tuning flags that can boost performance. We discovered that even these seemingly simple configurations exposed a surprisingly large and complex search space.
 The best optimization depends on the workload. Inductor exposes a freezing flag that tells the compiler that model weights will not change during inference. Knowing this, the compiler can transform the weights ahead of time to make subsequent computations faster. One such transformation converts weights to FP32 to perform certain optimizations, before converting them back to their original, lower-precision format. We found that enabling freezing improved throughput by 10–26% at larger batch sizes, where the GPU performs matrix-matrix multiplications. However, at batch size 1, where inference primarily uses matrix-vector multiplications, enabling the same flag caused a 49% slowdown . Upon inspection, we discovered that the FP32 conversion was not reversed for matrix-vector operations, leaving the GPU to process larger, 32-bit weights instead of the original lower-precision weights. In other words, the exact same compiler optimization could improve performance for one batch size while dramatically degrading it for another.

 Inductor config flags by quarter, 2022-2026 ‍
 Optimizations interact in unpredictable ways. As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year. These flags control everything from kernel fusion to memory access patterns and scheduling. Their effects are not independent: enabling the aggressive_fusion flag alone reduced Llama 1B throughput by 6 TPS, but enabling it alongside the combo_kernels , benchmark_fusion , and triton.coalesce_tiling_analysis flags improved throughput by 3 TPS. Even small configuration changes could produce measurable microsecond-level differences in execution time.
 Takeaway: the space of possible optimizations and configurations is large, and we should be searching it systematically instead of guessing the right flags to set.
 Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation isn't necessarily the fastest during inference.
 Inductor makes optimization decisions based on its benchmarking harness. We identify two distinct ways that this benchmarking misleads its decision, hurting overall performance as a result.
 First, it ignores that kernel performance depends on caching behavior. Torch Inductor clears the GPU's L2 cache before benchmarking individual kernels, but during inference, kernels often reuse data that is cached from preceding operations. We observed 39–58% slower timings in Inductor's isolated benchmarks than in the live forward pass, where cache reuse can reduce memory traffic.
 Benchmark inputs can also distort cache behavior in the opposite direction. For example, when benchmarking torch.embedding , Inductor initializes the tensor of token IDs to zero, causing every token to access the same embedding vector. For a 64K-token sequence, this made the kernel 2.1× faster than with random token IDs , due to artificially high cache reuse.

items.content:
All blog posts

 Inference

 Published 11/16/2026 

 Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads

 What the harness and the inference engine each have to get right so a long agent session stays fast for long horizon tasks.

 Authors

 Zain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)

 Table of contents

 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

 Summary

 Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps.

 Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more.
 This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache.
 We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike!
 What an agent turn looks like to a GPU
 Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it's a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out.

 A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls.

 So for agents, "how fast is this model?" mostly means "how fast can it get through a long historical account of pervious turns?" The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather then recomputing.
 Cache is king
 The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one.
 Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part.

 The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length.
 The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again.
 Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule.

 The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness.
 The harnesses and APIs
 On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows.
 Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring.
 Loading tools late
 Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it.
 Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you've starred to a calendar, and it searches for "calendar," loads the save_calendar definition, and calls it.
 For the cache, the question is where that definition goes.

 The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway.
 Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don't expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn't have to know this, but anyone building a harness does.
 Things at the top that change
 The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read.
 Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user's name or the date the session started, don't hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that's already cached, which we'll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere.
 Reasoning effort
 We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn't a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation.

 Let’s say you're deep into a long task and it isn't going well. You raise effort from low to high. That's a reasonable thing to do, but the next request now differs from the last one almost at the first token. Which means the whole session gets processed again. On a long run, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens spent on changing one setting.
 Our advice is to pick an effort level at the start and leave it there. If you really need more thinking, it's often cheaper to start a fresh session at the higher setting than to continue the old one, and you get a clean context out of it too. You could also compact before changing the reasoning value to decrease the amount of prompt tokens.
 Big tool results
 A tool’s output becomes part of the next request, and of every request after it. If the agent reads a 3,000-line file when it needed forty lines, you don't pay for that once; you pay for it on every remaining turn (even if it is cached you lose out on the context window). To combat this, harnesses often cut tool output down. That's the right call, but how you cut tool output matters.

 Here's a failure that's easy to build by accident. The task is to fix a timezone bug in a calendar export. The agent reads calendar.py , and the tool returns the first 100 lines of a 640-line file without saying it stopped. The function that matters, convert_timezone , is at line 420. The model has no idea it's missing anything.
 The fix is a single line in the output, telling the model it got lines 1 to 100 of 640 and that it can search the file or request another range. With that, the model searches for "timezone," finds line 420, and reads lines 410 to 450. Cutting output saves money. Cutting it without saying

 Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI.
 It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory.
 In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process.
 As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows.
 GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). 
 To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned.
 How we run agent evals at Together
 Building the task list
 Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint.
 By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example:
 List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. To pass the eval, the agent has to:
 Find the latest pricing info.
 Call the regions API endpoint to list the available regions.
 Combine the two to find the cheapest option.
 Produce a valid CLI command for creating the cluster.
 The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents.
 Three configurations
 After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways:
 Baseline: The agent receives just the prompt, with no special configuration, mirroring the average developer's workflow. It can use all its default tools, like fetching docs from the web, but we don't give it any specific MCP connectors or skills.
 MCP: The agent gets direct access to our documentation through our MCP server, so it knows exactly where to search when it hits a roadblock.
 Skills: We give the agent the Together skill package , which contains instructions and examples for using our services, written specifically for agents.

 When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it.
 Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back.
 Scoring a run
 After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts:
 Pass: Every task requirement was met.
 Incomplete: The agent attempted the task, but some required steps were unfinished or unverified.
 Fail: The agent gave up early, broke an explicit constraint, or produced an incorrect result (RIP).
 Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking.
 We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency.

 Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier?
 List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it. Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled.
 Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page.
 The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available.
 More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap.
 Isolating the failure
 To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill).
 We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API:
 Query GET <https://api.together.ai/v1/compute/regions > or run tg clusters list-regions --json for the live region inventory, supported instance types, and compatible CUDA/driver pairs. Open the GPU Cluster pricing table for current on-demand and reserved rates. After this change, the task passed 100% of the time for all models we tested using the skill-enabled config.
 Finding gaps in our API
 The same GPU task also turned up a problem in our API. In a recent baseline run, Opus 5.5 got an incomplete verdict, and the transcript showed it hitting two dead ends that were not the model’s fault.
 The run started well. The agent called /v1/compute/regions to retrieve the regions and instance types. Then, looking for prices, it called /v1/compute/instance-types , and the API returned a 400 with this message:
 Region is required. Example: us-central-8 . Use /v1/clusters/regions to get list of regions. So the agent did what the error told it to do:
 It retried the request with a region from its first lookup. Instead of instance types, it got a 404 .
 It called /v1/clusters/regions , the route the error suggested… but that route doesn’t exist, so it got another 404 .
 Our own error message had sent the agent to a route that doesn’t exist, and the retry that should have worked failed too. A developer following that message by hand would have been just as stuck. We’ve since fixed the error message to point to /v1/compute/regions , and the routing bug behind the first 404 .
 Case study 2: Rebuilding our skill package
 We used to maintain 14 separate Together skills, one per product surface. They were a pain to use: you had to know in advance which skills applied to your workflow, then install and invoke each one. The skills also overlapped, repeating the same SDK guidance and setup instructions, and each was long enough that loading a few of them in tandem could bloat the agent’s context.
